newsitem.title: USA: Dow Chemical cleared in Michigan implant case.
newsitem.headline: Dow Chemical cleared in Michigan implant case.

text.p: A judge ruled Thursday that Dow Chemical Co. is not liable for medical problems that hundreds of Michigan women claimed arose from silicone gel breast implants, the third such state court victory for the giant chemical company.

According to Dow Chemical, Wayne County Circuit Judge Robert Colombo Jr. rejected plaintiff claims that implant maker Dow Corning Corp. had relied on Dow Chemical to establish the safety of silicone for use in the implants.
Dow Chemical did not make silicone for the implants, although it says it did conduct silicone tests in the 1940s and 1950s for its co-owned Dow Corning venture that were unrelated to breast implants.

Dow Corning is jointly owned Dow Chemical and Corning Inc. Once the world's largest maker of breast implants filled with silicone gel, Dow Corning filed for bankruptcy-law protection from creditors two years ago because of the claims it was facing.

Appellate courts in New York and California have upheld lower court rulings that also said Dow Chemical was not liable. Herb Zarov, an attorney representing the company, told reporters during a conference call that Dow Chemical will next tackle suits in other states.
"Judge Colombo's opinion is part of an emerging consenus in state courts across the country that Dow Chemical should be dismissed from silicone gel implant litigation," he said.

The company said the Michigan decision affects about 800 cases filed against it in the state. More than 3,000 silicone implant cases against Dow Chemical in state courts have been dismissed, as well as more than 1,000 in federal courts.

The Midland, Michigan-based company continues to face a total of about 14,000 implant cases, with the majority of those under the jurisdiction of U.S. District Court Judge Sam Pointer in Birmingham, Ala.

Jury selection began earlier this week in New Orleans for the first phase of a Louisiana class-action lawsuit filed against Dow Chemical. Zarov said the case involves many of the same claims that Colombo dismissed in Michigan.
But the lead plaintiff attorney in that case said Colombo was not given all the facts, including documents that allegedly show Dow Chemical was involved in safety testing.
"We have crucial evidence never admitted in the Michigan court," said the attorney, Dawn Barrios.
David Black, one of the lead plaintiff attorneys in Michigan, said the women were disappointed.
"I'm sure we're going to seriously look at filing an appeal to the Michigan Court of Appeals," he said.

Thousands of women with silicone gel implants have filed lawsuits against manufacturers alleging the implants caused connective tissue and immune system problems, as well as other ailments. Manufacturers maintain there is no scientific proof of a link between the medical problems and silicon gel implants.
Unless Colombo's ruling is reversed, Black said it was likely that Michigan women will only have the bankruptcy case from which to seek remedies.
